strengths: The paper presents a genuinely interesting approximation to softmax attention: separate clustering of queries and keys, a two-stage residual refinement, and dipole/covariance corrections are well motivated and more original than many purely sparse or low-rank attention variants.

The manuscript gives a reasonably clear algorithmic description, including complexity claims for acausal and causal settings, explicit pseudocode, and an intuitive cumulant-generating-function derivation for the monopole/dipole approximation.

The microbenchmarks report full forward-plus-backward runtimes including clustering overhead, and compare against CUDNN Flash Attention and a Pallas Flash implementation. The reported long-context speedups are substantial in isolated attention layers.
The ablation table is useful: removing dipoles, two-stage clustering, or monopoles increases error, supporting the claim that the components are not cosmetic.

The end-to-end PG-19 pretraining experiment is a valuable sanity check showing that the approximation can train a small model without catastrophic degradation, rather than only matching isolated attention outputs.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main pretraining result is a single 29M-parameter GPT-like model on PG-19, with only one central global-attention layer and all other layers using local attention. This does not establish robustness across model sizes, datasets, architectures, layers, or realistic long-context pretraining regimes.

There is no reporting of variance, repeated runs, or statistical uncertainty. The headline 0.36% loss degradation and 12.2% runtime reduction may be within run-to-run or implementation variance, especially at this small scale.

The end-to-end baseline comparison is limited. The main 16k comparison uses the authors' Pallas Flash implementation rather than the strongest available exact-attention implementation in the same training setting, while CUDNN Flash is only shown for the 256-window configuration. This weakens the wall-clock claim.

The approximation errors remain fairly large in microbenchmarks: the chosen fast 64-cluster setting has relative squared error around 0.195, and several reported configurations exceed 0.20 despite the abstract's phrasing. The paper does not characterize how this error affects gradients, later layers, rare tokens, long-range retrieval behavior, or downstream quality.

The theoretical justification is suggestive but incomplete. The dipole derivation relies on a tilted covariance, but the implemented algorithm uses an unweighted per-key-cluster covariance and then aggregates it approximately. The resulting approximation order and error statement are not rigorously established for the actual algorithm.

The causal extension is only briefly described. The claimed O(NCD log N) behavior is plausible, but the paper does not provide enough detail about block scheduling, masking, memory traffic, backward pass implementation, or numerical stability to make the causal algorithm fully reproducible.

Reproducibility is limited. Hyperparameters are listed, but there is no mention of released code, kernel implementation details, random seeds, tokenizer training details sufficient to recreate the setup, hardware/software versions beyond A100, or exact benchmarking protocol.

The paper does not compare experimentally to other efficient global-attention methods such as Performer, Nyströmformer, Linformer-style approximations, Routing Transformer variants, or recent clustering-based inference methods adapted where possible. This makes it hard to place the speed/quality tradeoff in context.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are some rough edges and inconsistencies, including typographical errors, cramped extracted tables, and claims that are stronger than the presented evidence. The limitations section is effectively folded into future work rather than explicitly discussing failure modes, scaling risks, and cases where approximation error may be unacceptable.

Ethical concerns are minimal for the algorithmic contribution, but the paper gives little discussion of dataset provenance beyond PG-19/Project Gutenberg or broader implications of making long-context pretraining cheaper. This is not a major flaw, but the treatment is thin.

strengths: The paper contains a concrete algorithmic idea: approximating softmax attention by separately clustering queries and keys, then using a two-stage attention computation with monopole summaries and a dipole correction. This is more substantive than a pure systems tweak, and the motivation for treating query and key spaces separately is plausible.

The derivation via cumulant-generating functions gives some useful intuition for why covariance-like dipole terms can reduce approximation error, and the ablation table supports that the two-stage structure and dipole term matter for the reported approximation error.

The authors report end-to-end wall-clock timing rather than only asymptotic complexity, and include clustering/merging overheads in the microbenchmarks. This is a good practice for efficient attention work, where overheads often dominate.
The paper is reasonably readable overall, and the main algorithmic pipeline is understandable from the algorithms and figures.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not sufficiently supported. The end-to-end validation consists of only a single 29M-parameter GPT-like model on PG-19, with only one global attention layer and the rest restricted to a 256-token sliding window. This is too narrow to establish viability for transformer pretraining in the sense implied by the abstract and conclusion.

The training evaluation appears to report single runs only, with no variance, no repeated seeds, and no statistical analysis. A 0.36% loss degradation is presented as minimal, but without run-to-run variability it is hard to know whether the difference is meaningful, stable, or an artifact of this setup.

The comparison baselines are weak and incomplete. The main long-context baseline is the authors' Pallas Flash Attention implementation rather than the best available optimized attention stack for the full training setting. The paper also does not compare against strong efficient-attention alternatives such as Performer, Linformer/Nystromformer-style methods, block-sparse/local-global variants, or recent clustering methods in a comparable training setup.

The approximation quality evidence is limited. Microbenchmarks use recorded Q/K/V from one trained model and report relative squared output error, but do not characterize backward-pass error, layerwise effects, robustness across layers/checkpoints/tasks, or whether the reported 10-25% output error is acceptable beyond the one small pretraining experiment.

The causal extension is under-evaluated. The paper proposes a hierarchical block decomposition with O(NCD log N) complexity, but the end-to-end experiment uses a very specific configuration where only part of the causal matrix uses MuSe. There is little evidence about behavior at larger contexts, different block sizes, or fully stacked global-attention models.

The claimed speedups can be misleading. Large microbenchmark speedups at 64k are shown for isolated acausal attention under fixed total token count, but the actual pretraining speedup is only about 12%. The paper should more clearly separate isolated-kernel results from model-level gains and explain expected gains in realistic architectures.

The theory is mostly heuristic. The error discussion uses informal big-O arguments around residual query/key covariance and partially specialized dipoles, but does not provide a rigorous bound for softmax attention approximation, causal composition, or accumulated training error.

Reproducibility is inadequate from the manuscript alone. It gives useful hyperparameters, but there is no clear release of code, kernels, exact implementation details, random seeds, preprocessing/tokenizer artifacts, or benchmark scripts. For a systems-heavy attention method, these omissions make the results hard to verify or build on.

Presentation has some rough edges: several equations/algorithms have shape inconsistencies or unclear notation, the table extraction/layout is cramped in places, and there are typos such as 'desribed' and 'attenting'. These are not fatal by themselves, but they compound the difficulty of validating the method.

The limitations discussion is too thin. Important limitations such as small-scale validation, lack of broad baselines, dependence on custom kernels, approximation-induced training instability, and unknown scaling behavior are either only briefly acknowledged or deferred to future work. Research ethics concerns are minimal for this algorithmic paper, but compute/resource reporting and reproducibility details should be stronger.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely interesting and technically motivated approximation to softmax attention, combining separate query/key clustering with a two-stage semantic approximation and dipole covariance corrections. The distinction between query and key spaces is well argued, and the cumulant/multipole derivation gives useful intuition for why the approximation error should depend on residual query/key variance.

The empirical results are promising: isolated attention benchmarks show substantial speedups over Flash Attention at long contexts, and the reported pretraining experiment at 16k context obtains a meaningful step-time reduction with only a small final loss increase. The ablation in Table 3 supports the importance of both the two-stage structure and dipole correction.

The presentation is mostly clear and self-contained. The algorithms are described concretely, complexity claims are stated, and the appendix gives enough model and optimizer hyperparameters to understand the main pretraining setup.

The contribution is significant if it scales: a drop-in global attention approximation that preserves training quality while reducing wall-clock time would be useful for long-context pretraining, and the paper provides an encouraging proof of concept rather than only synthetic timing results.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still narrow relative to the strength of the claims. End-to-end training is shown only for a 29M parameter model, on one dataset, with only one global attention layer while all other layers use local attention. This makes it hard to know whether the method remains stable and beneficial in standard larger transformer pretraining regimes.

The pretraining evidence appears to be based on single runs without error bars, seed variation, or repeated trials. A reported 0.36% loss degradation is small enough that run-to-run variation could matter, so the central quality claim is not fully established statistically.

The runtime comparisons are promising but somewhat specialized. The end-to-end comparison uses a Pallas Flash Attention implementation for the global 16k baseline rather than the fastest available production kernels, while CUDNN is used only for the local-window baseline. This weakens the practical wall-clock speedup claim.

Approximation errors in the microbenchmarks are fairly large in relative squared error terms, especially for the fastest configuration used later. The paper argues these errors are acceptable empirically, but gives limited analysis of backward-pass error, training stability, downstream behavior, or failure modes across attention heads/layers.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript provides hyperparameters and algorithmic details, but I did not see code release details, kernel implementation specifics sufficient for reproduction, hardware/software versions beyond a single A100, or enough information to independently reproduce the custom Pallas kernels and clustering behavior.

Limitations are acknowledged mostly as future work on scale and optimization, but the paper would benefit from a more explicit limitations and ethics/research-impact discussion. There are no major ethical concerns apparent, but the resource and deployment implications of accelerating long-context pretraining are not discussed.

strengths: The paper proposes a technically meaningful and fairly original approximation to softmax attention: separately clustering queries and keys, using query-conditioned exponential tilting, and combining cluster/block summaries with exact retrieval. The method is well motivated by the residual expansion of the attention score and by the invariances of query/key spaces.

The empirical evaluation is substantially stronger than is typical for efficient-attention papers. It includes attention-layer microbenchmarks, end-to-end 64k-context pretraining up to 1B parameters on both code and scientific-document data, scaling experiments from 96M to 1B, comparisons to exact CUDNN/Pallas Flash Attention, comparisons to MoBA, and evaluations on pretrained Llama 3.2-1B and Llama 3.1-8B without retraining.

The ablations are useful and directly tied to the claimed contributions. Tables separating monopole-only, retrieval-only, query-clustering, cluster-count, block-size, retrieval-count, head-dimension, and context-length effects make the main mechanism more convincing than a single headline speedup/loss result would be.

The practical contribution is significant: a reported 2x isolated attention speedup and 36% end-to-end throughput improvement at 64k context while preserving loss is valuable if reproducible, especially because the method is positioned as a drop-in approximation rather than a new architecture.

The paper is generally well presented. The method overview, pseudocode, clustering details, hyperparameters, data construction, optimizer settings, and hardware setup give a clear picture of how the system works and what was measured.

The authors are reasonably candid about some limitations, including limited larger-scale validation, head-dimension coverage, kernel optimization status, and the need for exact-attention fine-tuning in one 1B code setting.
weaknesses: The reproducibility story is incomplete for a systems-heavy method. The method depends on custom JAX/Pallas kernels and CUDA K-means kernels, but the manuscript does not state that code or trained checkpoints will be released. Without implementation artifacts, reproducing the speedups and even the exact approximation behavior would be difficult.

Several headline quality claims are based on very small loss differences, often framed as MuSe 'beats' exact attention. Differences such as 0.7001 vs 0.7026 or 1.6166 vs 1.6201 may be real, but the paper gives no repeated runs, confidence intervals, seed variation, or statistical treatment for pretraining loss. These should be presented more cautiously as parity unless variance is quantified.

The evaluation scale is strong but still short of the broad claim that the method is ready for long-context pretraining generally. The largest trained model is 1B parameters on a single 8xA100 node, with mostly head dimension 64, no GQA/MQA implementation, and no experiments on modern multi-node training regimes where communication, load imbalance, and kernel details could alter the throughput story.

Comparisons to baselines are somewhat narrow. MoBA is the main approximate-attention comparator, while other relevant long-context training or sparse/global attention methods are mostly discussed but not empirically compared. The MoBA configurations may not reflect optimized or production settings, and the paper itself notes that its own kernels are not fully optimized, making wall-clock comparisons hard to interpret cleanly.

The long-context-utilization evidence is suggestive but not fully decisive. Loss-vs-position curves show models benefit from later positions, but there are no targeted retrieval, needle-in-haystack, code-repository, or document-level tasks that would test whether MuSe preserves specific long-range dependencies rather than aggregate language-modeling loss.

The method has complexity and engineering risks that deserve deeper treatment: streaming K-means in fp16, capped balanced assignment, per-head independent summaries, and per-batch clustering could introduce instability, load imbalance, or domain sensitivity. The paper reports favorable settings but gives limited failure analysis beyond the no-tilt case.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. There are no material ethical red flags beyond standard LLM pretraining concerns, but the manuscript does not explicitly discuss data licensing/privacy risks for The Stack v2 or scientific PDFs, nor energy/compute implications despite focusing on pretraining efficiency.

strengths: The core idea is interesting: separate query/key clustering with query-conditioned exponential tilting is a plausible and original way to improve centroid-based attention approximations.

The paper gives a fairly complete algorithmic description and includes useful ablations on query clustering, cluster count, retrieval, block size, monopole-only variants, and pretrained Llama compatibility.
The reported systems results, if reproducible, are practically meaningful: about 2x attention-layer speedup and 36% end-to-end throughput improvement at 64k context on 1B-scale pretraining.
weaknesses: The evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Main quality claims rely mostly on custom code/PDF pretraining losses with tiny reported margins over exact attention, no variance across seeds, and minimal downstream evaluation on only ARC-Easy/SciQ.

The claim that MuSe 'matches or beats' exact attention is not fully convincing: improvements are very small, likely within training/evaluation noise, and the 1B code result requires brief exact-attention fine-tuning to remove an adaptation gap.

Reproducibility is weak. The method depends on custom JAX/Pallas/CUDA kernels, clustering details, data filtering, and hardware-specific choices, but there is no clear code release, implementation checklist, or enough detail to independently reproduce the speedups and training results.

Comparisons are incomplete. MoBA is the main sparse baseline, but the paper does not convincingly compare against a broader set of optimized long-context training alternatives or production-quality sparse/linear/global-local attention implementations.

The limitations discussion is too brief. It does not adequately address sensitivity to hardware, kernel maturity, sequence parallelism/ring attention in practice, larger model scales, training stability, or whether the method remains beneficial beyond the specific 64k/1B/single-node regime.

The ethics/data treatment is insufficient. The paper uses large code and scientific-document corpora but does not discuss licensing, privacy/PII, copyrighted content, or downstream risks of accelerated pretraining.

strengths: The paper presents a meaningful and technically interesting approximation to softmax attention: separate query/key semantic clustering, query-specific exponentially tilted summaries, and exact retrieval of high-mass cluster/block pairs. The motivation is clear, and the decomposition into monopole approximation plus retrieval is well explained.

The empirical evidence is unusually strong for an efficient-attention paper. It includes microbenchmarks, ablations isolating query clustering and tilting, comparisons to MoBA at matched sparsity, 64k-context pretraining up to 1B parameters on two domains, scaling from 96M to 1B, and checks on existing Llama models.

The headline results are practically significant: about 2x attention-layer speedup and 36% end-to-end pretraining throughput improvement while matching or slightly improving validation loss. The adaptation gap when switching MuSe-trained models to exact attention is identified and tested via short exact-attention fine-tuning.

Presentation is strong overall. The method overview, algorithm, tables, and appendices make the approach understandable, and the paper gives many implementation and hyperparameter details, including clustering, block sizes, optimizer settings, datasets, and hardware.

The limitations discussion is honest about model scale, head dimension coverage, kernel optimization, and grouped-query attention. I did not see material research ethics concerns beyond the usual compute and dataset-provenance issues for language-model pretraining.
weaknesses: Reproducibility still depends heavily on custom Pallas and CUDA kernels, and the manuscript does not clearly state that code will be released. Given that the contribution is partly systems performance, independent verification may be difficult without the implementation.

The evaluation scale is good but not definitive for modern long-context pretraining: the largest model is 1B parameters on one 8xA100 node, mostly with head dimension 64 and a particular alternating local/global architecture. It remains uncertain whether the same quality/speed tradeoff holds for larger production LLMs, GQA-heavy architectures, or multi-node sequence-parallel regimes.

The claimed drop-in compatibility with pretrained models is promising but somewhat narrow. The Llama evaluation focuses on per-position loss on PG-19 chunks rather than downstream long-context tasks, generation quality, retrieval/needle-style behavior, or robustness across domains.

Some empirical claims rely on small loss differences, often a few thousandths of a nat, where run-to-run variance is not reported. The paper would be stronger with multiple seeds or confidence intervals for the main pretraining comparisons.

The MoBA comparisons are useful, but the implementation/budget details leave some ambiguity about whether the baselines are fully optimized and tuned under equal engineering effort. This matters because the paper makes both algorithmic and wall-clock performance claims.

The method introduces several interacting hyperparameters (query/key cluster counts, retrieval counts, block size, spatial retrieval), and while the appendices include ablations, guidance for choosing them under different sequence lengths, model sizes, and hardware settings remains incomplete.

strengths: The paper proposes a technically interesting and fairly original approximation to softmax attention based on separate query/key semantic clustering, query-centroid exponential tilting, causal block accumulation, and exact retrieval of selected cluster/block pairs. The method is well motivated by an error decomposition: separate query clustering preserves more of the query-key interaction than key-only clustering, and the ablations support this mechanism.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an efficient-attention paper: microbenchmarks, component timing breakdowns, ablations over cluster count/retrieval/block size, comparisons to MoBA at matched sparsity, 1B-scale pretraining on two domains, scaling from 96M to 1B, pretrained Llama drop-in tests, and long-context retrieval/downstream checks.

The main practical result is meaningful: roughly 2x isolated attention speedup and 36% end-to-end pretraining throughput improvement at 64k context on 1B models, while maintaining comparable loss. The paper also checks interchangeability with exact attention, including the observed adaptation gap and a short exact-attention fine-tuning mitigation.

Presentation is generally strong. The algorithmic description, figures, pseudocode, complexity discussion, and appendices make the method understandable, and the paper includes useful implementation details such as clustering, balanced assignment, optimizer/model/data settings, and hardware.

The limitations and impact discussion are reasonably honest. The authors acknowledge limited head-dimension coverage, kernel optimization status, larger-scale open questions, RULER weaknesses, and possible societal risks from cheaper long-context modeling.
weaknesses: The strongest quality claims rest on very small loss differences, often favoring MuSe by 0.1-0.4%, with no apparent multiple-seed training runs or confidence intervals for pretraining loss. This makes it hard to distinguish true regularization benefits from run-to-run noise, especially when claiming that MuSe 'beats' exact attention.

The evaluation scale is substantial but still limited relative to the claims about long-context pretraining. All main training is at up to 1B parameters on a single 8xA100 node, with 64k contexts and mostly head dimension 64. It remains unclear whether the method behaves similarly for larger frontier-scale models, GQA-heavy architectures, longer contexts, or more diverse data mixtures.

The method is implementation-heavy, relying on custom JAX/Pallas and CUDA kernels, segmented flash attention, clustering kernels, and careful memory/index handling. Although code is said to be in supplementary material, it is described as research code rather than maintained implementation; reproducibility and adoption may be challenging.

The comparison set is somewhat narrow. MoBA is the main training-time sparse baseline, and some MoBA settings are chosen to match MuSe sparsity rather than to maximize MoBA's own quality/speed tradeoff. More comparisons to other modern long-context training approaches or optimized baselines would strengthen the significance claim.

The adaptation issue is not fully resolved. The default MuSe-trained 1B code model degrades when evaluated with exact attention before fine-tuning, and the proposed non-differentiable aggregation fix is described as preliminary and identified late. This is important because drop-in interchangeability is one of the paper's central selling points.

The long-context capability evidence is mixed. RULER results are poor for both MuSe and exact-attention models, and the stronger custom NIAH benchmark is in-domain and specifically constructed around code imports. This supports the absence of obvious degradation but does not fully establish broad long-context reasoning or retrieval competence.

Some claims about future speedups are speculative. The measured end-to-end gain is 36%, while larger gains are attributed to better kernel optimization and far-field sparsity. The paper would benefit from clearer separation between demonstrated speedups and optimization potential.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck: making global attention cheaper for 64k-context pretraining without changing the model architecture. The proposed query/key semantic clustering with query-dependent tilted summaries is a plausible and reasonably original extension over spatial blocking and key-only clustering.

The empirical package is broader than many efficient-attention papers: isolated attention benchmarks, ablations of query clustering/retrieval/block size/cluster count, 96M-to-1B scaling, two domains, pretrained Llama compatibility tests, and downstream/code retrieval evaluations.

The main reported efficiency/quality tradeoff is practically meaningful: about 2x attention-layer speedup and 36% end-to-end throughput gain at 1B/64k while roughly matching exact-attention losses. The ablations support the claim that query clustering mainly improves summary quality rather than retrieval selection.

Presentation is mostly clear, with helpful pseudocode, figures, and appendices. The limitations and impact statement acknowledge some real issues, including adaptation to approximate attention and restricted scale/head-dimension coverage.
weaknesses: The central claims are still narrower than the framing suggests. All main pretraining experiments are at <=1B parameters, on a single 8xA100 node, with mostly head dimension 64 and a specific alternating local/global architecture; it is not yet clear that the method remains beneficial for larger modern LLMs, GQA/MQA-heavy architectures, distributed long-context training, or more optimized exact-attention baselines.

The comparison to MoBA and other efficient-attention methods is limited. The matched-sparsity setup may not reflect each baseline's best operating regime, and the paper does not provide a strong apples-to-apples comparison against optimized implementations or other current sparse/approximate long-context training methods.

The end-to-end speedup claim depends heavily on custom Pallas/CUDA kernels and hardware-specific implementation details, yet the code is described as supplementary research code rather than maintained infrastructure. This reduces reproducibility and makes it hard to judge whether the reported wall-clock gains will transfer.

There is an adaptation/interchangeability issue: the 1B code MuSe model degrades under exact attention before fine-tuning, and the proposed non-differentiable aggregation fix appears preliminary and discovered during review rather than fully integrated into the main experimental protocol.

Long-context capability evidence is mixed. RULER results are mostly poor and attributed to domain shift/instruction-following limitations; the custom NIAH benchmark is in-domain but author-designed, and some large MuSe-over-baseline gains are surprising enough to need stronger controls and analysis.

The theoretical analysis is useful for intuition but not a strong guarantee: it relies on residual-size and isotropy-style assumptions, loose covariance bounds, and heuristic K-means behavior under tilted distributions. It does not tightly characterize failure modes where semantic clusters are unstable or attention is highly adversarial/sharp.

The limitations section is relatively brief given the scope of claims. It should more directly discuss memory overhead, kernel complexity, sensitivity to clustering hyperparameters, numerical precision issues from fp16 clustering, and data/task regimes where the approximation may fail.

strengths: Original and technically interesting approximation: MuSe combines separate query/key semantic clustering, query-centroid exponential tilting, causal spatial accumulation, and selective exact retrieval in a way that is well motivated by the residual expansion of softmax attention.

Sound empirical case: the paper reports 1B-parameter 64k-context pretraining on both code and scientific documents, with a 36% throughput gain over CUDNN Flash Attention and comparable or slightly better losses in the main settings.

The ablations are unusually informative. Tables separating monopole vs retrieval effects, query-clustering vs no-query-clustering, cluster count, retrieval budget, block size, and head dimension make the central claims much more credible.

The method appears practically relevant: isolated attention speedups are near 2x, the approach requires no architectural change, and evaluation on pretrained Llama 3.2-1B and Llama 3.1-8B supports the claim of drop-in compatibility when tilting is used.

Presentation is clear overall. The paper gives useful pseudocode, implementation details, hyperparameters, datasets, hardware, and extensive appendices, making the contribution easier to understand and reproduce than many systems-oriented attention papers.

The authors treat limitations and risks reasonably, including adaptation to approximate attention, limited scale, head-dimension coverage, kernel optimization needs, and broader misuse/accountability concerns.
weaknesses: The strongest evidence is still limited to 1B models, 64k context, and a single 8xA100 training setup. The paper argues for long-context pretraining broadly, but does not empirically demonstrate the method at multi-billion or frontier-scale regimes where communication, memory layout, GQA/MQA, and production kernels may change the tradeoffs.

There is a real interchangeability caveat: on 1B code, MuSe trained with the default setup degrades when evaluated with exact CUDNN attention before fine-tuning. The proposed 0.1% exact-attention fine-tune and the non-differentiable aggregation variant are encouraging, but the latter is described as preliminary and not part of the main runs.

The main speedup comparison is somewhat narrow. CUDNN Flash is a strong baseline, but comparisons to optimized implementations of other sparse/clustered methods are limited, and the MoBA comparison is partly constrained by matched sparsity choices and the authors' own kernel setup.

Long-context downstream validation is mixed. RULER results are poor for both MuSe and exact-attention models, and the strongest retrieval evidence comes from a custom in-domain code NIAH benchmark; this is useful but less independently established than standard long-context evaluations.

Reproducibility is adequate but not ideal for a systems contribution: the paper says research code is provided as supplementary material but not as a maintained implementation, and the method depends on custom JAX/Pallas/CUDA kernels whose exact performance may be difficult to reproduce across stacks.

Some claims about broader scaling and future speedups are plausible but not fully established. For example, the paper shows approximation error trends with context length, but explicitly leaves longer-context speedups and recursive/local-block optimizations to future work.
